utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld, you have something to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Just before my friends recommence with the cross-examination, I just might say that our trial support people have come up with a document, a two-page document which appears to be in about six languages showing a measurement conversion table for all kinds of things including square metres to square feet and other conversion documents. This may be of some assistance to everyone including myself since I have difficulty with the conversion. My friends have no objection to that being provided to the Court, and hopefully for the balance of our witnesses, we will try also to provide some additional information to the Court during the course of the trial to assist in the conversion, but this is a start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ryneveld. The document has been provided to us, and we will be forever indebted to them. Mr. Petrovic, it's your turn.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I begin?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Petrovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning Witness A, my name is Vladimir Petrovic, and I'm representing Damir Dosen. In your testimony so far you mentioned that in the 1970s, in 1972, I believe, you served with the Yugoslav Peoples' Army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will, please, the counsel and the witness pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you tell us briefly what was it like in the unit that you served with?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You are being asked to observe a pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So could you, in a few words, describe to me the organisation of your unit from the point of view of discipline, the relationship between the soldiers and their superiors? What was it like at the time when you did your military service?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1972 I was drafted in my town in Prijedor. I was a driver with the army. I served in Benkovac. I spent three months attending a driving course. I drove a tractor M-5 for the 155-millimetre howitzer. All three peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina served the so-called Yugoslav Peoples' Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell me from the point of view of discipline?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Discipline was strict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell me what that means?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: You had to be disciplined. You had to execute your military tasks in time. If you failed to do something, you would be punished, and the rule was execute and then complain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After your return from the JNA, did you become a reservist like most other people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a reservist in Banja Luka, in the Kozarac barracks, and I twice attended military drills refreshing my knowledge at Manjaca but at that time I was not a driver anymore. At that time I was engaged as a marksman, a shooter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, at the time when you were invited to attend these drills as a reservist, was the discipline again as strict as at the time that you served in the army of Benkovac or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: The discipline was not the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the difference?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: The difference was that we did not have to be clean shaven or did not have to have a tidy haircut. That is, perhaps, the principle thing I can say now. And we were joking and buggering around while, when you did your regular service, you had to have your hair cut, you had to shave every morning so that was the difference.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if you can, please, will you compare in terms of discipline and apply it to Keraterm? That is, did the guards who guarded Keraterm, did they look to you like a disciplined unit, regardless of the type of unit they were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you that they did not behave as if they cared much about discipline.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you mind explaining it to us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that they were very -- they threw their weight about. At times they would wear camouflage trousers and an olive-green grey shirt. They were -- they did not shave, did not wear -- were untidy, ill-treated people. I don't really know what to tell you, with the exception of individuals who treated prisoners correctly. And before this Honourable Court I must say that, and I said this about Kajin's shift and Kole's shift, and the two of them, even though even amongst their ranks, there were some undisciplined members but when they were around, nothing could happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if I understand you well, when you say "undisciplined," it means they disobeyed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I should like to go back to -- no. Just one more thing. So you were -- you spent those two months or slightly over two months in Keraterm. Did you have the impression that the orders there were issued in the same manner in terms of the chain of command as in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please describe it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as you know, in JNA whoever is reporting has to stand to attention, make three steps, raise his hand, salute, report, and at the end of the report, if it is, for instance, let us take a lance corporal or captain -- if a lance corporal is reporting to his captain, at the end of the report, they would shake hands. And after that, they would again salute and then he would either turn right or left, and then the lance corporal could leave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we can then conclude that that did not exist in Keraterm, far from it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, far from it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I should like to go back to the time when you were arrested on the 31st of May, is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me if you know - of course, if you don't, then you won't tell me that - but persons who arrested you, and persons who guarded Keraterm later on, did you have the impression that they were one and the same unit or were they two different structures?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if we look at it, there were some people who arrested and others who guarded the men in Keraterm. Those men who arrested me I never saw them in Keraterm even.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I am correct, you mentioned a man whom you saw also at the time of your arrest and in Keraterm and you called him Joja?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was the only one there. And Your Honours, there was a village next to Bosanski Novi, that is the village was called Agici and Joja came from Agici and he asked, "Is there somebody from Agici?" Two teachers reported and the next day two people disappeared from dormitory two.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Joja came to Keraterm a few days later and took out two men from Room 2?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you're not right. It wasn't a couple of days. It was two days later. And if I am allowed to describe to the court how it happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, tell us briefly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: He entered the dormitory, Room 2, took his rifle off the shoulder, put it beside him and sat down with us. And said, "Is there somebody from Agici here?" So two men responded. And he asked them, "What are you?" And they both said they were teachers. Then he said, "You're all going for interrogation and those who are not guilty of anything will be released, and if anyone is guilty of anything, I shall shoot him with my own hands." And I never saw that man in Keraterm again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you see those two men whom he --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never saw them in Keraterm again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Joja was not a member of any of the guard units, of any of the guard organisations in Keraterm, is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned on various occasions a man whom you called Tomica. Could you describe him to us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Tomica worked with Janic at Ambalazerka and I went there every morning to get the merchandise. Well, if not every day, every second day. He was short, stalwart, I would say sort of medium height.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was he? Was he a guard or was he one of those who came there from time to time, at shorter or longer intervals, to Keraterm? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is very difficult to say who was the guard in Keraterm, very difficult. Apart from the commanders, very difficult to say who was the guard, a proper guard there, because those -- all those who wore uniforms, be they camouflage or the olive-green grey uniforms, they could all enter the compound.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On various occasions during your testimony you mentioned that there were people who prevented the entry of those various uniformed individuals?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you also confirm before this court that Kajin was one of those who did his utmost to prevent those men from entering the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell to the court very honestly and truthfully, whenever Kajin was present on his shift, and whenever he was in the compound, then the likelihood of incidents was very slight. He was very correct. What I do hold against Kajin, and what I saw often, is that he would often take his motorbike or his car and leave the compound of Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you perhaps recollect one of those incidents when Kajin drove away one of those visitors, if I may call them that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were many such occasions when Kajin was there. There were many such situations. They come, "Come on, give us a man. We need him." And he would never let them, especially in daylight. At night -- and I repeat before this Honourable Court when he was present, that nothing could happen, but I say again before this Honourable Court, that at times Kajin was wont to leave the compound, that he would take his motorbike or his vehicle and simply leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, could the witness clarify why he held it against Kajin that he would leave the compound, that he would often leave the compound? Why did that bother you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: It bothered me. It bothered me not every time, but mostly whenever he left the compound, and then there would be an incident. Some outsiders would come, call out, beat, and there was nobody to stop them. And I believe that Kajin been there, those things would not have happened because it was a correct shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us now try to establish something about the number of the detained in Keraterm. In the beginning when you came, you said you were the first ones, that there was nobody else in Keraterm at the time when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many people were there in Room 2 because that was the only room at that time, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the only room at the time, Puharska, and I shall explain to the Honourable Court, Puharska is a suburb locality with about 800 Muslim households. In Puharska there were less than two per cent of Serbs, our neighbours. When the buses arrived to pick us up, some of the buses went through Marica directly to Omarska, and as far as I can remember, two buses, and I and my brother, were in them and yet another bus, we went through Kozarac because this is a shortcut. And when we arrived in Omarska, we were taken back to Keraterm. As we entered it, the hall that is Room 2 was empty. That is the first night, there were about two buses with some 50, 60 men each which means roughly about 120 men that night. The next day they brought people from the town, many of whom I knew. They also brought more people from Puharska, from Gornja Puharska. They also brought people from Cerici so that in three or four days' time, the room was full. Three or four days -- after three or four days, there were about 450 men in that room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you mentioned the figure of 1.350, if I am correct. So when did the detainees reach that figure?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was about 15 or 20 days later that we reached that figure. When we, from Puharska, were in the camp, I can tell the Honorable Court the exact arrival of Sivci, that is how they arrived, village by village, how people were being brought to the camp. If the Honorable Court wishes me to do so, I will tell you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is no need to go into all that, and I should like to go back to the time of your interrogation. Do you remember if on that day or the next day, you talked to Kajin, what was it that you talked about, and what did Kajin tell you what was your task?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can, yes. After I was arrested and some 11 or 12 days later, following my brother[redacted] , I was also taken for interrogation. And then we returned to Room 1 because allegedly it was -- there was interrogated one room, and those yet not interrogated another room. A day or two later, Kajin, since he knew me, he told me, [redacted]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And why did he pick you out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I suppose because he knew me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there were other people there, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you now describe briefly the room that you were kept in, that is, first Room 2 and then Room 1? What I want to know is what has not been elicited so far, that is, when you are in the room, when you are behind the door, what can you see from Room 2 or after those 11 or 12 days, what could you see from Room 1?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Room 2 you could not see anything, and I am saying this before the Court, except when the door was open. And they allowed to keep the door open because the lower part of the door is an aluminum plate but above it are windows. From Room 1, until they put those additional bars there, because it was very hot, I can tell the Honorable Court that the temperature was between 37 or 38 degrees and at times soared up to 40 degrees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So could you see something through those windows? You tell us that it was aluminum and then above it was windows, so what are those windows?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were glass panes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you could see through them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could see through them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in Room 1?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Room 1 there was an identical door with some -- after 25 days of interrogation, men came from Bosno Montaza. They brought those bars, and they welded those bars there and a small door. So welders came, but they were not proper welders. And Saim Balagic, who was a professional welder, one of those knew him and invited him to help him do that. So he did both those doors in Room 1 and Room 2 and his award was half a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. cigarette.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now tell me, from Room 1 looking from right to left, and you must still have this picture in your head; what do you see to the right? Do you see the Keraterm fence? Can you see the road behind it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see the main road and the fence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On your right-hand side?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I stand like this, then to the right, yes. This is the Prijedor-Banja Luka Road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in front of you, you can see the area between dormitories 1 and 2, the weigh hut, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And in front of Room 2 and in front of Room 1, you can see the gate, you can see the weigh hut.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your field of vision covers this whole area in front of Rooms 1 and 2, in front of Room 1 and more to the side. And shall we make it clear to the Court, what can you see in the direction of Rooms 3 and 4?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the directions of Rooms 3 and 4 you can see this grass area, the park, and the lamp post. That is, you can see practically the whole Keraterm yard except just one small part which is at a dead angle and that you can't see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So to all intents and purposes, from Room 1 you could see the whole area in front of four dormitories?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You cannot see this whole area, but from the asphalt area which separates those dormitories because there is a path, then there is a park, that is an asphalt path, and over there you can, again, see the park. And you could see it with the naked eye, all of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time when you arrived in Keraterm were there some booths for the guards?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were machine-gun nests set up with canvas over them, and around them there were two large boulders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But were the booths supplied later?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that there was a booth in front of Room 1, in the direct view of Room 1?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you were, shall I say, [redacted] [redacted] it that way, did ever any commander of the shifts request from you to collect money or valuables, I mean Kajin or Kole?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. Not a single shift commander even Fustar, even Fustar in there, and his men and they were the worst. Even they did not do that. But I once did have to collect some money and give it to a soldier whom I did not know. And I suppose he was never even a guard in Keraterm. Once again I repeat to the Honorable Court that in the Keraterm compound, all, whoever wore a military uniform, a Muslim could put on such a uniform, and whoever put on a uniform could enter the compound because nobody has Serb or Croat on Muslim written on his forehead, and we all look alike. We are all humans.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, you told us about the organisation of shifts in Keraterm. Do you recollect if, in the beginning, during the first ten days or a fortnight there were two shifts, and then later on --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember. And those shifts did not -- were not on duty for 12 hours, but on -- but for 24 hours. I can tell the Honorable Court that nothing was properly organised at the time when we arrived. You simply didn't know who was in command, who had to do what. And then it was some five or six days later that the shifts were introduced. So in the beginning everybody did as he pleased. There was no organisation at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in those early days, let us go back to that. Did you ever notice the army guarding Keraterm rather than -- those men who came later?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, every night, every night, not by day, but every night. Every night, the TO, the so-called TO would come to reinforce the sentries around, and I saw there some Kole, I saw Fustar who cried[redacted]when he saw me, when he saw Sutka, when he saw Saeb. He said, "Look at Cucar, look at Herga." I apologise to the Court, but I can't just watch it. I can't do that. And he just turned on his heels and never came back. Fustar brought a loaf of bread to split it amongst us and also shed some tears and said, "I didn't have more money to buy any more, take it from me, I'll never come back again here." And those are our friends, Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But we are not referring to Fustar who later on became a shift commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. That was a man who worked for Trgo Prodaja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said yesterday that you had known Kajin before the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the war he was not a policeman; do you know this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You certainly know that people who provided security for -- in Keraterm were reserve police officers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know what they were, whether they were the reserve policemen or they were military. The only thing I saw was Gruja, who was wearing a police uniform. He was a wonderful man. Occasionally he would give us cigarettes. He would sometimes swing the baton to -- as if he were going to hit someone and then he would just put it down and said, "I never hit anybody. I won't do it now." He would come at night as reinforcement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that in addition to the regular guards, at night other persons also joined in the guard duties, you said, like Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me, in Room number 4, let's say until the middle of June, maybe even beyond that, what was in that room, do you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that room, there was -- there was various goods.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any Serb prisoners in Keraterm during that period, if you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you mentioned that in some shifts, the doors to the rooms were being locked. Why? Why was it important to have the doors locked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: The doors to the room, when the additional bars were welded on, padlocks were put on. That was about 20, 25 days after we came in. I think that this was done for our safety so that no one who would come in would be able to walk in and beat people, which is what used to happen before the padlocks were put in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the doors locked in Kajin's shift?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you said about difficult conditions in -- prevailing in Keraterm. Do you remember a situation, some situation in which Kajin helped some men being transferred to the hospital for treatment? Do you remember something like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please expand on that answer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Sengin was beaten up. Several people were beaten up. I'm not going to say that it was -- whether that was Kajin's, Kole's or Fustar's shift, but a van arrived and then they took these people to be treated, and then they were brought back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were they taken, to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that people had a lot of lice at that time. Do you remember whether anybody came to give them some powder against lice or somebody came to give men the haircut?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mica, who had an arm missing, came to help people who had dysentery, to give them tablets. Even I went there even though I was not suffering from dysentery. Fortunately a soldier approached me and said, "What do you want?" I said, "I need tablets." And he said, "Go back to your room." Whoever had come for these tablets received beatings and that came on the orders of Mica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was somebody put in charge of giving inmates haircuts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was people -- we did it among ourselves. This was done in front of Room number 4. There was a man who would just shave people's heads.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned Ziga and Duca yesterday. Can you tell me about Ziga? Was he a guard or was he somebody who would come from outside, or was he perhaps first one and then the other?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not like to offend people but whatever I would say about Zigic would not be enough. He was a murderer. He was a rover. He was all over town. At one stretch he did not sleep for three days and three nights. Who could do that? If -- it was nothing for him to kill a person. He was enjoying his bloody deeds. He seemed to be on drugs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, Ziga and Duca were bullies. They freely entered the Keraterm and they just did whatever they wanted to the prisoners, including killing Serbs, if they want to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right, sir. In order to satisfy their instincts, they would even kill Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they listening to anyone's orders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no one's orders. They did whatever they wanted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you mentioned that together with Drago Tokmadzic, somebody else was also beaten. Can you tell us who this was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Drago Tokmadzic and Spija, I remembered the name of my colleague, and it is Kole's colleague. He was a driver. When I -- when his wife came to deliver some food and he asked, "Where is Spija?" And I said, "He was killed." And then he hit his head against the pole and he said, "Who did this?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, you said that Goran Lajic had done it, a man from Fustar's shift?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know his first name. Drago Tokmadzic was a policeman and Lajic worked in a coffee bar that worked all night. When all the other places were closed, we would all go there, to that bar. And he told Lajic once, "It's time for you to go home." And when he -- and when Lajic was beating, he was reminding him of what he had told him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you saw Lajic beating Tokmadzic and the reason why he later ran away?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At one point yesterday you said that Kajin apologised for what he did. I'm going to remind you of a situation, and tell me if that is what it was in reference to. After the event in Room 3 when he threw away his pistol and he apologised to you in front of Rooms 1 and 2, is that the incident?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But do you recall what I'm trying to remind you of now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please tell me what that was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: That night Kajin left, if I -- his duty post, if I can call it that. Several people were taken out and beaten up. When Kajin returned, probably some of the guards told him what had transpired. Kajin came in front of Room number -- Rooms number 1 and 2. Your Honours, believe it or not, the man was in tears. He was cursing and yelling, "Who did this?" And cursing their mothers. "Is this what could happen?" Again, let me say, regarding Kole's and Kajin's shifts, when they were present, when Kajin did not leave, nothing happened. If only everybody was like that, had been like that, not that many of us would have perished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This was before the Room 3 incident?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Maybe go on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me take you back to the events that followed your release from Trnopolje. I understood you to have said yesterday that Kajin, with two other men, one was Dugi and there was a third man came to visit you as a friend?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was almost nine years ago now. Many details of that conversation you have probably forgotten. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will never forget it, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What will you never forget?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: What happened in the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, I apologise. I'm referring to the Kajin's visit to your home. I have no doubt that you will never forget what you experienced in the camp, but the details of the conversation you held in your house, would you allow that perhaps after nine years some details may be forgotten?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course they can. If one is capable of forgetting them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I'm putting to you, sir, is that Kajin told you that he had not taken part in the attack on Kozarac but that he passed through Kozarac after the attack on Kozarac. Would you allow that this could be what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can say to Their Honours is verbatim what Kajin told me then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You knew Kajin's father well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what kind of a man he was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a wonderful man. He was a noble man, a family man. This was a honest family in that regard. My colleagues -- Kole and Kajin were my colleagues. We all socialised. I never once felt that they hated Muslims or vice versa. I would like this court to find the real culprits, those who ordered in Prijedor to -- for all this to happen. There were 30 to 40 per cent of mixed marriages in Prijedor. I never distinguished between the Muslims and Serbs and I had more Serb friends than Muslim. I cannot fathom how this could have happened in my town. This was Kozara. Kozara was famous in World War II. Everybody defended the old Yugoslavia together, both Serbs and Muslims. And now, they are fighting each other. Had Muslims wanted to do this to the Serbs, then I would have congratulated Serbs for having event --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who, sir? Who is the culprit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Zeljaja Kuruzovic who taught our children this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness A, would you like a moment to compose yourself? Perhaps have some water?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you in a position to continue now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to those whom you mentioned, are there others whom we should see here in -- instead of the ones who are in the dock?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Srdo Srdic was the SDS president. And this was a party of that -- of those who were whipping up hatred. I used to live in Nurija and I was looking for Muro, [redacted]. And he is asking me, "Where is Muro?" And I didn't tell him where he was -- didn't tell

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the witness has mentioned his first name twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The last thing I have to ask of you, the one that is here today, you had known him before the war, you knew him at Keraterm? What do you know about this man keeping in mind what you have just told us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are asking me for my opinion not only about Kajin, but the entire family, it was an honest family. It was a working family. This Kajin socialised with Muslims. The only thing I object to Kajin, and this is what I am saying in front of these Honorable Judges, why did he have to leave his shift? Why did he have to get on his motorcycle and go? I don't know what the reason was, but as soon as he left, there was trouble. I'm saying here publicly to Their Honours, I never saw in Keraterm camp that Kajin hit anyone, that he mistreated anyone. But I am not going to say about what other people saw. I am saying about what I saw.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, perhaps, that several weeks before Keraterm, Kajin lost a child?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that means that you did not know anything about his personal problems at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vucicevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Vucicevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness A. I know that this is very difficult for you. This is why I will start with questions which probably will bring back memories of moments that may have been slightly different from the most of what you experienced in the camp. Yesterday you said that occasionally your father would bring you food; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, in addition to your father, your wife also was bringing food?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, she came on one occasion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this during Kole's shift?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that occasion did your wife personally hand you the food?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can tell Their Honours how this happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With Their Honours' permission, will you please do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If it's necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: I think it is necessary. It goes to the mens rea, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will you please say what happened on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [redacted] each other and if not, whatever." My wife didn't do it. When I came -- when I went out and kissed my wife, Kole took the rifle, point at me and said, "You can go back." And I said, "What are you doing, Kole?" And he said, "Don't worry, old man, you'll be all right soon." And I want to thank him for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before you go on, Witness A, please remember you are here under protection, and one element of the protection is that you have the benefit of a pseudonym. So your name should not be mentioned, neither should your nickname. So please avoid references to your name or nickname.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you gave evidence that your father would come quite frequently to deliver food and that he also was doing it, for the most part, during Kole's shift; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, my father also came during other shifts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, during -- on one occasion, if you remember, your father brought something and, in fact, either you or someone else wanted to give this to Kole as a present; do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not remember that. I don't remember that we wanted to give Kole a present. I only remember on one occasion during Kole's shift, my father had brought some food, Kole personally took it, brought it to me. I said, "Could my father bring some extra food during your shift?" And he said, "You can bring as much as you'd like. I will take it." I told my father, "Please go and buy as much bread as possible."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my apologies. I just noticed that my client has been taken out to the hospital [sic] to compose himself. I would request to perhaps take a quick break and then continue. This was very emotional testimony for him too. I believe that he should be present during the rest of the testimony of Witness A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It has been brought to our attention that your client needed to go to the bathroom and we were in agreement with that. We don't think it is absolutely necessary to take an adjournment if he's going to be away for a very short time. Let me consult with the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we are of the view that if he is away for a short time, say ten minutes, we'll continue. If he's away for longer than that, then we'll just take an early adjournment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't know. He came out in tears. May I leave the courtroom and see what is going on with him and I can come back and inform the Trial Chamber? So may I have your leave to do that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, sir, you testified about an incident that a flag from the mosque was brought into the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you testified what Kole did to a Muslim inmate who attempted to burn this flag?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you didn't tell us what Kole did with that flag afterwards. If you remember, can you say what he did?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kole kicked him, this little Aco. He said, "Take this flag and put it away there." And that day that flag was sitting there. After that I never saw it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vucicevic, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, too. Can I ask for a ten-minute break, and after that he will be able to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, we are sensitive to the request that you have made, and mindful of the provisions of the Statute which provides for the accused to be present during his trial. We are not encouraging motions of this kind, but what we'll do is we'll take the break now and return at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I wish to apologise once again for the interruption, and I wish to say that Mr. Damir Dosen's counsel are fully aware of all the statutory provisions, and if you deem that necessary, we are quite ready to obtain reports from the detention unit about the mental health of our client and the treatment he is undergoing, and which I believe has to do with what happened today and which explains why and how it happened today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We don't think that that is necessary at this stage, Mr. Petrovic. I should say that we will take the luncheon adjournment a little early today at 12.30, resume at 2.00 and have a slightly longer afternoon session until 4.15, with a very short break at an appropriate time. Mr. Vucicevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, the lavatory facilities in the Keraterm factory and subsequently Keraterm camp, you were detained there, you used the same facilities, didn't you, as the workers who had worked there before that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct. There was one lavatory and we all used that one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, this one lavatory, did it have several bowls or was it a squatting facility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was -- there were three squatting facilities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, to urine -- for urination, there was separate facility, rather primitive, with just a small conduit and a low wall; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. That was the shower booth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that five, six, seven men could relieve themselves at the same time there, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As for water, drinking water, and for the laundry or refreshment, you used water from a water pumps, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I must add for the court, in the early days, those fire water pumps were not fitted properly for us to use that water so that we fought over them, and depended on shifts. There were some barrels and there was a van. Tomica drove it. And Kole allowed water to be brought to the camp and be distributed among the detainees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The shortage of water in the water supply system, or rather as you call them, water pumps, there was a shortage only when the power was cut, was off, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We used them only when they fitted up properly because a hose was brought and it was a hundred metres long and during Kole's shift and Kajin's shift, too, we would wash ourselves, we could refresh ourselves, pour some water into plastic bottles and take them to our dormitories, because these two shifts did not ban us from -- did not prohibit us from taking water into dormitories.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to that, there was also water -- this matter of supply with water, the military would bring water cisterns to the camp, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Some 15 days before we were to leave the Keraterm, yes, a fire cistern came and there was another grey painted cistern. I do not know which company in Prijedor it belonged to, and there was also a yellow painted one which came from the public utilities company. I know the Serb driver from this public utility service which brought it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the driver of that cistern or water tank, was it -- were they civilians or were they military persons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: The drivers wore uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember what uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were olive-green grey uniforms. They were not camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they those were military uniforms, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the name of the driver? I believe you mentioned it, the driver who brought the water?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember his name but he lived not far from where I lived, some 400 or 500 metres away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I thought you knew the name but this is also a very satisfactory answer. Thank you very much. However, these days in the summer of 1992 were very hot, you already testified about this, do you remember if Kole took groups of detainees to a well in the neighbourhood to get some water?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did say so already when we arrived, the hydrants were not fitted yet. There was not a hose so that one could use the water. They didn't -- didn't know what to do with us. And there were a couple of large plastic barrels, and there was a van there. I remember it well. And Tomica, with Kole's permission, and a couple of prisoners would go to fetch that water. I never went to fetch that water, but those who did know were those wells were. This water was icy, and that's why I believe that it came from natural wells.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to drink that water?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did have an opportunity to drink that water.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As regards food, in the early days when you arrived, that food, bread was unloaded as you told us at a corner, at the corner of Room 2 and that other part of the building which juts out. However, a few days later, if you remember, the food -- they began to bring food by trucks; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the bread was also brought at different times of the day, but it was not unloaded at that place any longer, it was left on the upper floor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember if the detainees took part in the slicing of bread which was brought in loaves?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where was that bread prepared for distribution to the detainees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had the opportunity of seeing it personally and even being present there. The bread was sliced, and as soon as the door would be opened next to dormitory 2, there was a table and bread slicer. And I think that that slicer belonged to the Keraterm personnel, [redacted]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those two women who distributed food, they also worked there Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. as cooks, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did. There was a shorter one, her name was --

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me for interrupting, I have to butt in. [In English] With your permission, Your Honours, because we intend to call one of the ladies that distributed the food, and she will be a protected witness for her wishes. That's why I didn't want her name to come out. The witness has testified that he knows them, and if I explain do you know why I interrupted him because I didn't think it would be something that would be proper with the view on protection of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, that was quite appropriate. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, you said that you knew those two women who were distributing food. Are you aware that one of them is married to a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The name of her husband is familiar to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. So one of them is married to a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: My friend, yes, a friend of mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when those two women distributed food, did they treat you roughly or did they distribute the food normally as they used to do in the workers' canteens beforehand?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm speaking about myself. No, they did not treat me roughly because they knew me. And I should like to seize this opportunity to say, I feel I have to do that, that that -- the wife of this friend of -- this Muslim friend of mine, brought two kilograms of sugar to me and Avdo Drljaca who was there and who was a male nurse and he was one of us, that sugar saved the life of many of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified that during Kole's shifts nobody was ill-treated. I should like now to draw your attention to some specific details. Did you ever see any detainee being beaten in -- while queueing for food on Kole's shifts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw that during Kole's shifts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you have heard of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I suppose I would have heard of any such incident during -- from other detainees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you never heard from any detainee that somebody was ill-treated while queueing for food?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never heard that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you testified about Kole gave out food that was brought for guards, but how he gave that food to weakly prisoners, to sickly prisoners. Did he do that himself or did he ask you, [redacted] [redacted], to select the detainees who would be given that food? If you remember that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: He never asked me to select the prisoners who would need that. I saw Kole on two or three occasions bring soldiers -- mess tins and I would see him come to the -- to dormitory 2, and would call out those under age and those hungry and tell them, "Come out and get this food."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said how one of the soldiers on an occasion kicked those vessels with food. Was that one of those soldiers who brought the food?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not think so. Kole would bring this food, put the mess tin down, go back to his hut, and they would sit there. There would be a fire because they would have something roasting there and they would be eating, perhaps drinking. I could see some alcohol there so they may have been drinking. And once this food was kicked off, I do not know whether Kole saw that or didn't. Whether he could see it or not, I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But at that time, as you testified yesterday, is that you believed that had Kole seen that, he would have prevented that or punished those who had done that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no doubt about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that guards prepared -- that the guards had roasted a pig on one occasion -- not on one occasion, on various occasions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you also help them on one such occasion to prepare a lamb? I believe it was a lamb, to prepare a lamb that they would put on a spit and roast?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you present next to the fire as the lamb roasted?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not present even if they tried to keep me there but I went to the dormitory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And before you went to the dormitory, did Kole offer you something in reward for what you had done?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: He asked me to take a piece of that pig, of that lamb, and have it, and I said I could not. So I took a beer and I gave it to Said Hrgic. And later on, afterwards, I saw Aco and Ilko carry a large slice of meat and eat it, and they even brought it to the dormitory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you talk to Kole on various occasions, on many occasions? Did you talk with Kole while he served as a guard in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you even several times sat with him on a bunker next to the machine-gun, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true, but I wasn't sitting there alone. There was another guy who was called Dudo and another one was called Said. We were quite free. Kole would take off his shirt to get some sun tan and we could chat. At times he would give us a cigarette or two. We talked and he disagreed with things that were going on in Keraterm, and I'm quite confident about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. So your testimony today on the basis of these numerous conversations that you had with Kole was that he disagreed with the things that went on in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That I'm quite positive. And I can vouch for that before this Honourable Court. And let me say one more thing, I am sorry because some people lost brothers, fathers, whole families, and it happened during Kole's shifts and I'm really sorry that these things happened during Kole's shift, and it is very difficult to say anything -- it is very difficult to defend any of those things, but I'm here to tell the truth, and I will speak only the truth and truth only, and rest assured that I am speaking the truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, when you mentioned that fatal night, the first thing you said yesterday was that when the gun-fire started, Kole ran to the place that you pointed to us yesterday. Where was it that he came from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: He came from the hut. I saw him running, turning, shouting, cursing, "Fuck you. Don't fire in this direction. Stop the fire. Give the hose to men in the room." But nobody listened to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness A, Witness A, you again used the word "in this direction." Yesterday you also said "in this direction." And you said it two or three times. However, to make it quite clear, what the words "in this direction" mean in our language -- I should like to give you a few examples, and if you agree, you please tell us so and if you disagree, again tell us so. If I said we, the Defence counsel, are in this direction, and the Prosecution are in that direction, would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that will be correct to my mind, but at that moment, since there were some stray bullets, at that time his words was, "Don't fire in this direction," but the moment he said, "Break the window. Give the water and the hose to men," then naturally, it had to do with dormitory 3. At least that is how I see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. So a man who in one breath says, "Don't, stop fire," curses at those who are firing and he says, while the fire -- while there are flames about, "Give them a hose," you do not understand this as his giving orders to open fire on Room 3? He is requesting that all shooting stop at any of the rooms, at all the rooms, because otherwise you cannot put a hose in without stopping the fire, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. And I believe, and I think, and I'm positive, that Kole meant Room 3 and that he wanted to prevent what then happened. I repeat to the court once again, I wish it happened during Fustar's shift because it was the worst of all of them, but I repeat, during Kajin's shift and Kole's shifts, I wish everybody was like them because, in that case, very few out of us would have perished and there wouldn't be trucks taking away the dead every day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us just go back to some more general matters. There were no callouts on any night when Kole's shift was on duty, that is nobody was called out and ill-treated during his shifts; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. One -- on one occasion, it happened a stray soldier, if I call him that, came from the road - from where, I don't know - and he was there and asked that somebody come out from the dormitory. I forget the name, and then Kole did not allow that, and that soldier said, "Well, then, I'll open fire on the dormitory," and Kole got his automatic rifle and said, "Yes, friend, if you open fire on a dormitory, I'll open fire on you."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Kole was quite ready to fire at a Serb in order to protect men he was guarding, his townsmen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, hearing what -- having heard what Kole said, I'm quite sure that he would have done that, because for Kole, for Kajin -- Kole and Kajin did not distinguish Muslims from others because they socialised with Muslims quite often. And I should also like to point out, because this is not the end, I shall give you more answers, I should like to hear from them, I should like to hear it from them, who ordered -- whose -- who did the orders come from to do to Prijedor what was done? It was from Srdic, from Zeljaja, who did all sorts of horrific things around places, who did no end of harm to the Muslim people.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I find that at certain moments the witness is going a little broader, but being that he is a victim and very emotional to him, I would relinquish that respectfully to you if he needs to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I had a specific question to raise. I didn't quite follow the point that you were seeking to make when you asked the witness about a special meaning in your language of "in this direction." Witness A, I'd like to ask you quite plainly, when Kole said, "Don't fire in this direction," did you understand him to mean, "Don't fire in the direction of Rooms 1 and 2 but direct your fire at Room 3"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is not how I thought. Let me repeat. Kole said, "Don't shoot over here." There were stray bullets, because these stray bullets were going in the directions of Rooms 1 and 2. At that same time without stopping, he said, "Break the windows, stop shooting, and put in the hose in the room." Your Honours, that was in reference to Room 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In an interview that you had with the OTP investigator, Mr. Smyth, on the 16th and 17th August, you gave evidence where you quoted an instance when Kole came during another shift to save a prisoner who was being beaten; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber how this happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: One night, several people were called out to be beaten. I recognised the scream of [redacted]. His last name was Seferovic. His father was a baker. Suddenly I saw Kole running in the compound. He said, "What are you doing? You go back into the room." And he said it rather curtly. And people went back in. So further mistreatment and beating was prevented. I never saw Kole in another shift. I don't know how he came there that night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified that whoever was wearing uniform could come and enter the Keraterm camp. Did this happen during Kole's shift?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they would come.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the people who would come in during Kole's shift, could they mistreat prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I remember once during Kole's shift Dusko Celica entered the room and they said, "Celica, go out." And he said, "I'm better with Ustashas in here than with you Chetniks out there." This is what Dusko said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anybody abuse him because of that joke?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the -- during the notorious shift, what would have happened to such a person, can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one could say what would have happened to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you testified about the beating and murder of Professor Hergic. Would you agree with me that this happened on 24 July in the course of the day, that is during the day shift, that is, in the period of between 6.00 in the morning and 6.00 in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot recall the date. I said that we did not know what day of the week it was; Monday, Tuesday, Friday. Believe me, I had -- I kept no track of the days, let alone dates. I cannot recall the date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But if you will remember, you testified that this happened during the day, and during the night was when the incident in Room 3 took place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This did not happen on the same day. Besim was killed when people from Brdo were brought in and unloaded next to the scales on the grassy area. That's when Besim was mistreated. And these men were then locked up for 10 or 15 days before they were all killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the day when the massacre in Room 3 took place, of course your testimony is that this took place during the night, but during that day, was there any mistreatment of prisoners during -- on the eve of the massacre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall, and I don't remember whether there was any mistreatment, but I believe there was none.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that day, the room -- the door to your room was closed at dusk like any other day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the door but the bars. The door was open. The door was opening on the inside, and then the bars were welded on and there was a door in that -- that barred part with a padlock.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember whether Kole that night closed the door at dusk like any other night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified that between 4.00 and 4.30 in the afternoon on that day, you saw a power generator in front of Room 3?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did see it, but not in front of Room 3 but across from the Room 3, across from the grassy patch and the asphalt walkway on the grass. If necessary, we can have the picture of Keraterm back, and I can point exactly the place where these power generator and the two school desks were placed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you talked with Mr. Smyth in your home in August, you said that you had seen Kole after Keraterm was disbanded, and you said that there was a car which had a Brcko licence plate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was a black Volga car.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, what is the licence plate letters for Brcko?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the letters of B and C with a diacritic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Prijedor's licence plates?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: P, D.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When Kole testifies he will say that he never drove a car with Brcko licence plates. It was indeed a Volga make, but with Prijedor licence plates. Is it possible that during your conversation with the investigator you may have thought that Kole was transferred to Brcko as punishment and that this idea in your mind made you think that the licence plate which you saw on the car that he was driving was carrying a Brcko licence plate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not possible. I'm going to explain to the Trial Chamber Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. these licence plates. When a person buys a car in Zagreb, within one month he has to transfer the registration locally in Prijedor and take local Prijedor licence plates. I never said that Kole went to Brcko to kill people. Maybe he bought a black Volga there, but the black Volga did have these licence plates when I saw him, B and C with a diacritic which stands for Brcko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday you testified that at first there were three shifts, and today when Mr. Petrovic asked you, you recalled and said that at first there were two shifts and later on three shifts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. For several days there were only two shifts which had up to 24-hour duties. But later on when they got better organised, there were three shifts working from 6.00 to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that at first, while there were only two shifts, Kole was only a guard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree with you, because for several days everybody was guards until they restructured themselves so that there was some semblance of organisation there. So that there was -- somebody was a commander and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether there were shift leaders at first when there were only two shifts? And if you do, who were these individuals?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At that point the organisation was practically zero.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this the period when most of the beating took place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: More of those incidents took place than after they became organised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, while Kole was on duty, was he always in the camp, he was not absent?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall well that Kole was present, but I don't know whether he was leaving the camp or not, but when he would leave, his deputy Batan would carry on with the tasks as honestly as Kole did. And for the rest, you know what happened to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember that once Kole went to take a prisoner home to visit his family and to take a change of clothes, if you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We will deal with that. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, without naming any names, mentioning any names, can you say whether Kole allowed a man whose father was killed that day outside of the camp to go home and use the phone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did. This man was in my room.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Kole know this man? Did he know him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you could say that he did and not, because I think Kole was older. They were not the same generation. I don't know whether he knew him or not. I cannot say before this Court, but I can say that I had never seen him in the same group with Kole.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But because his father had been killed on that day by the military in the area, this man waited for Kole to come on duty so that he could use the phone that night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you think that Kole did whatever he could to make the conditions of the detention in Keraterm as easy for you as possible?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe whatever Kole was capable to do, but I don't know what his capabilities were and what his authority was, but he fought for our well-being and our peace. Had he not done so, he wouldn't have said -- if he had let us out, he would not say, "Quickly go back in," and he would not push us into the room. And I said, "Why?" He said, "Soldiers are coming by and they may shoot you." And indeed, ten, 15 minutes later, soldiers would be passing on a road, Banja Luka-Prijedor Road, in trucks, and they were shooting in the air and singing. There would be howitzers that they were having on the truck. And Kole would say, "Please go in, go in." The door was narrow. It wasn't easy to go in quickly. I thought, is he crazy? And I say, "What is this?" And he said, "A convey would pass so you have to go in." And as soon as the column passed, he would again let us come out.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld, re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just have one area with about two questions for clarification. It was something raised yesterday during Mr. Greaves's cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. Re-examined by Mr. Ryneveld:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness A, I would just ask for clarification as to what term that you would use to describe the position in the camp or the function of people like Fustar, Kajin and Kole? What is the word you use to describe their position in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their position in the camp would be that they were commanders of their shifts. However, I never saw Kole, Kajin or even Fustar wearing any military insignia, whether they were corporals, lieutenants, captains, no military insignia on their uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By the same token, I'm going to ask how you would describe the position in the camp held by Sikirica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would describe it as follows: Sikirica had working hours. He would come in the morning at 7.00, he would go home at 4.00. I never saw Sikirica in the camp at night. I personally never saw him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I'm asking for, sir, is the description, the word you would use to describe his function or position in the camp, not a description of his duties, but what word you give to that role that he played.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a word, he would -- he would ask of Kajin, Kole or Fustar if there were any needs for prisoners, to give them names of people who were going to be turned over to those who interrogated them. I can also tell to the Trial Chamber that there was a notebook in the weigh hut --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Try again, Mr. Ryneveld.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps I'll approach this this way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During a question that was asked by you yesterday by Mr. Greaves about an incident where Mr. Sikirica was asking for volunteers after the Room 3 massacre, you indicated something to the effect of it would start from Sikirica, 15 volunteers, then commander would pass it down to us. "Question: Did you mean by that that Sikirica passed on the request for volunteers to the commander? Answer: Yes. Question: Thank you. And to make it absolutely plain, by that answer you mean that Sikirica was different from the commander?" Do you remember being asked those questions and giving those answers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that is certain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. When you refer to the commander in that case, to whom were you referring? What people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I say "commander," I am referring to a person who can issue orders. I don't know how to explain this to you but let me try it in this way, and this is my opinion. Sikirica, in my opinion, during his working hours, was the superior to Kole, to Kajin, and Fustar, as these shifts switched, during his working hours. After his working hours, the responsibility was to be taken over by Kajin, Kole or Sikirica. This is what the order was supposed to be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, you've just said "Kajin, Kole or Sikirica." Did you mean to say "Sikirica" the last? You said "after his working hours," referring to Sikirica --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS A [Resumed]
