But be that as it may, they really couldn't reason; they were beyond themselves. They were frightened out of their senses. And many of them still cannot really give a proper account. Those who did know, those who saw it, they are dead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did you discuss Kole's role in the massacre with anyone from Room 1 who would have been in a position to see and hear what was going on that night?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There were guys who saw that and they also heard Kole saying, "Don't fire in this direction." And he stood in front of the room which was least protected, Room 1, because it was wide open. There were no walls so that bullets could enter the room directly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, Witness, you indicated that you were taken from Keraterm to Trnopolje. Do you recall approximately what day that was and approximately how long you remained at Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I was taken to Trnopolje on the 5th of August and I spent 8 days in Trnopolje until the 13th of August, that is, and then I was released, but I was told that I had to sign papers whereby I would be leaving all my property to Republika Srpska. And I was also requested to leave Republika Srpska immediately. Those were the conditions under which they could release me from that camp, from Trnopolje. And my parents, my family did it for me. They got those papers for my brother and for myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution has no further questions for this witness at this time, but before I sit down, I just wanted a clarification with respects to Exhibits 3, 4, and 5 that those have, in fact, been admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, they have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Greaves, with the kind cooperation of the interpreters, I think we can go to 4.30. Cross-examined by Mr. Greaves:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness B, can I just first say this to you, please: Please listen to my question and then just answer the question. It will make it much quicker for you if you do that. Second thing is if you don't understand my question, please tell me straight away and ask me to repeat it or rephrase it. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness B, can you tell me a little bit, please, about this: Prior to the war which broke out in 1992, did you participate on an active basis in politics in any way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since the war, have you participated actively in politics?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or contributed money to political parties in any way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Heaven forbid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you now, please, about your military service. You did your national service presumably when you were a young man; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And without being specific about the dates, would that have been sometime around the end of the 1970s?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: That was in 1980 to be exact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've served subsequently in the military forces of your country, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From when to when?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Could you clarify this question? Does it -- do you mean the country before the war or the country since the war?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After your release from Keraterm and Trnopolje, you served in the military forces?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from which date until which date did you serve in the military forces?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Must I answer this question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I served from the day of my arrival in Travnik from Prijedor, and that was the 29th of September until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as you are concerned, when was the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: The end of the war was on the 22nd of April when the hostilities were terminated. That is when all of us who were not professional soldiers became civilians again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No, that was in 1996.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this correct, that the branch of the service, and I assume that that was the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this right: That the unit in which you served was a unit which might be called a special forces unit engaged in covert operations behind enemy lines; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No, it is not correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you engaged in acts of sabotage?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I did not engage in sabotage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since the war, or indeed during the war, did you at any time work for the security services or intelligence services or police services of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. The time periods that Mr. Greaves is referring to are well after the time frame that's alleged in this indictment. I fail to see the relevance of this witness' participation in any government position after the time alleged in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think we'll allow him to go a little further. It may go to credibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour has identified exactly what the point is, and there's a good reason for it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness B, it's right, isn't it, that in the mid-1990s you made a number of statements to the security services of Bosnia-Herzegovina; do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: This is correct, yes. About this case, about the Keraterm case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Help us about this: After the defendant in this case, Dusko Sikirica was arrested, you were contacted by a newspaper, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes, Dnevni Avaz.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how it was that they got hold of your name out of the many hundreds of people who were in Keraterm? Did they tell you that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: They did. They called Sanski Most radio. That is Muslims were seeking information. They were trying to find somebody who could tell them something about Sikirica, and somebody told them that I might be one of those. And that was how they came by my number, and I could not really tell them anything specific, nor did I really want to tell them anything. Whether they did write a story, whether they published anything, I haven't the slightest because I never even read the papers then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on now, if we may, please, to the 30th of April, 1992. That was the date, was it not, when the Serbs took over the opstina of Prijedor. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Which date?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 30th of April, 1992, Witness B.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I think that is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Without telling us where you used to live, did you live actually in the town of Prijedor or in a village outside?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: In the suburbs, in Donje Puharska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in April of 1992, were you in employment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Between the takeover of the opstina by the Serbs and the date of your arrest, were you able to continue to move freely about Prijedor, obviously with checkpoints and so on having been set up, but apart from that, were you able to continue to move freely?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Well, I moved about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the end of May, 1992, is this correct, that there was military activity and fighting in the Prijedor area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it correct that there was fighting between forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I wouldn't call it the forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I'd much rather call them men who were defending their homesteads.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this correct, that following upon whatever sort of fighting it was, the Serb authorities began at that point to round people up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: The Serb authorities began to round people up after they had cleansed the villages with little resistance, that is Kozarac, Marina Brdo, the one up there, and following the attack on Prijedor, that is when they began to cleanse us. We had all turned over our weapons, I mean from the TO, from the Territorial Defence. We also had reserve police. The regular -- a regular unit -- well, I suppose that there are such units the world over. That is, nobody did, at his own initiative or something. It was under -- by statute, we had this territorial Defence and the reserve police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you take part in any of the fighting that you've described, whether it's defending your homesteads or whatever? Did you personally take part in that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the area in which you lived, the suburb in which you lived, it's right, isn't it, that the people who were arrested were only those who were of military age and who were male? Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I don't know if a 94-year-old man is militarily able.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the majority, the very large majority, of those arrested, they were military-aged men whom the Serbs considered to be dangerous to them. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Well, yes, you could put it that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And indeed, it is in precisely that way that I have put to you that you told the Office of the Prosecutor in August of last year in a statement which you made to them. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I remember answering their questions, and I told them how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness B, when you were arrested, is this correct, that you were told that the purpose of your detention was in order to carry out an interrogation of you and of the others who were detained?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time when you were arrested, how many others were arrested and transported with you to Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I'd say between 300 and 350. Well, perhaps less than 400, but something of the order of 300, 350.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And apart from some who were over what you would consider military age, those people in those -- you were transported by bus, is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people on the buses, men, again, all of military age, therefore no children, no women, no people who were physically disabled from being in the military?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: There were those under age. There were also disabled. Nobody asked you, "Are you disabled or not?" They simply see that that man was not too old and he'd be taken along.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you got to Keraterm, were there any detainees there before you, or were you the first?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I've already said so. There were five or six.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during the course of that first day, did others -- were others brought in from other areas of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: On that first day they were not brought there. It was -- it was only us from Puharska and from Cejreci, which is a village above ours. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness B, when you got to Keraterm - you had worked at the premises before the war - did it show any signs of being essentially any different from the building which you remembered?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No. This building looks as it should, but it seems to me that there were some corrections made.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You'll have to help us as to what exactly you mean by "corrections," Witness B. I don't think that's entirely clear.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Here, the entrance into Rooms 3 and 4, to the lavatory, there were some doors -- there was a door. Now I don't see it. It seems to have been covered or something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Compared with the building upon which you had worked before the war, were there any signs of any sort that any preparations had been made to receive large numbers of detainees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: No, there weren't. I wouldn't say so. It was empty, and that is I think why they put us there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From what you were able to observe in the first few days of your detention at Keraterm, was it your impression, your conclusion, that it had been opened as a detention facility without any sort of organisation or preparation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I believe it was prepared in advance because there were buses there, there was a unit rounding up one street, another unit rounding up another street. They knew exactly whom to take along.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's in relation to the people who were being detained. I was talking, Witness B, about the building itself and the nature of the organisation in the first few days.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I did say that the building was not built for the purpose -- for that purpose. A factory was built as a factory. It was a factory and worked as a factory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the sense of organisation, in other words, organisation of personnel, were you able to gain such impression of that as to whether that had been organised in advance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Well, I suppose it was. Because one cannot go and know strictly what his area of responsibilities or what, unless he received instructions from somebody. So I suppose I do not have such knowledge. I wasn't one of them. I wasn't planning that so I cannot know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was no food for the first couple of days; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And for a short period, it's right, wasn't it, that families were able to bring food to the camp and that was brought through to the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: That's right. But it lasted only for a very short time, only until Bajram, and it was only a few days later. On Bajram we did not get such food. We got nothing on Bajram.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to turn now to a particular individual, I want to know whether you know anything of him. Does the name Zivko Knezevic mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Zivko Knezevic?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. A man probably aged around 60 or so, a former policeman.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes, I've heard -- I've heard that he was the warden of the camp or at least responsible for it. Now it came back to me when you said that he was a policeman. Yes, I've heard it. I didn't have any such knowledge, but that is what I heard, that he was responsible for the detainees in this Keraterm, that he was the man in charge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: If Your Honour will just give me a moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Help us about this, please, Witness B: That person, Zivko Knezevic, did you know him in such way by sight at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I don't know how he looks even now, to date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear from other detainees of his presence in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: As far as I know, he did -- if he had come, I probably would have seen him or probably even met him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just help me and clarify, please. The question that I asked was did you hear from other detainees that he was in the camp or that he had been seen in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I heard that he was seen in the camp. Had he been there constantly, I would have known. So he came occasionally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was throughout the period in which you were detained there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I think that I was detained there almost from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Let me clarify the question for you, Witness B. You heard of the visits of Zivko Knezevic taking place throughout your period of detention; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes, something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But he did say, Mr. Greaves, "occasionally". I'd just like to clarify exactly what his evidence is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I don't think I've disputed that. I just wanted to clarify over what period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness B, can you help me, please, about this: You've told us about a man called Jovo who was a Serb who was killed whilst at Keraterm. Are you able to help us about such other Serb prisoners who were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: The question is unclear to me. Are you referring to the prisoners who were ethnic Serbs?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you told us earlier is that there was no other Serbs that were kept as prisoners at the camp.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: From what I know, there was only that one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall being interviewed by the Office of the Prosecutor and making a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor in January 1995, Witness B?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you remember at the end of making the statement, signing all the pages and acknowledging that the statement was true to the best of your knowledge and recollection?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I believe that that was so, yes. Perhaps I do not recall something. A number of years have passed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what you told the Office of the Prosecutor then was that there was a third room which contained Serb military prisoners and that those prisoners -- I'm sorry, that when more prisoners arrived, the Serb prisoners were moved to an office area as there were only about 10 of them. Do you recall telling that to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Let me clarify. I said something but not that. These Serb prisoners, those who were in the Serb detention were in Room 4. And from Room 4, they were moved to the back of Keraterm where a detention facility was made for them. And this is what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Witness B, during your evidence when you were answering questions from Mr. Mundis, I suggest to you that you first of all indicated that there were no other Serbs at Keraterm, and that was not true, not truthful evidence. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: How do you mean there were no other Serbs? You mean -- you mean what -- when I referred to Jovo?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. When you were giving evidence about Jovo, you told the Tribunal that there were no other Serbs at Keraterm. You were trying to conceal the fact that there were, in fact, other Serbs there, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I did not try to conceal that. I gave it in a statement so that is a proof that I wasn't trying to conceal anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why were these people being kept at the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: One was taking money. He was from Jelovac. I know -- I was in their detention facility. I was cleaning there. I knew two of these detainees so I exchanged a few words with them. Jugo and Cvarak were there so they know who these men are. Kajin also knows because he was there when this Jugo arrived, and the man from Jelovac was in the bus and he asked for money and he hit me. This is why he asked for that. You probably know why people get detained better than I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can now remember quite a lot about these people, Witness B. Just help us again. Why exactly did you not tell us about them earlier when you were asked by counsel for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: That question was not that important. I was talking about the crime and the inhumane acts. This was something on the side, and I have omitted that they were moved to other room, and that was the room where I went with my men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it because you were trying to emphasise in some way that this was simply a place for detaining Muslims or a Serb who had voted for the SDA? Is that why you didn't tell us about them earlier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: For someone who may have voted for SDA or not, which was the case of Jovo, this happened a month and a half later. This has nothing to do with that room and with the detention of those Serb soldiers, those soldiers who were detained but then quickly released.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move on. The people who were detained at Keraterm, would you help us about this, please: On average, how many people were detained there at one time throughout your stay?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: On average, there were about 1100 and 1300 men that were kept at Keraterm at any one time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And throughout the period of your detention and their detention, would this be correct, they were wholly in the power of the Serb authorities in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Whom are you referring to? The detainees?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The detainees, Witness B.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Certainly, they were wholly under the authority of any Serb in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would you also accept this, that during that period of detention, those people could have been killed at any time en masse by those very same Serb authorities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: I think that they could have done that. If they killed some, they could have killed all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the beginning of your period of detention, Witness B, some detainees were interrogated and subsequently released. How many were so released?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Those who were released numbered 100 to 140.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those people were issued with some sort of pass which enabled them to move freely about Prijedor; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B
utterances.text: Only in the -- within the limits of the town itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I'm about to move on to another topic, which will not take two minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. We will take the adjournment now. Before we do, Mr. Ryneveld, there is a matter I wanted to raise with you. I believe in your opening you referred to common enterprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Does the Prosecution case of a common enterprise, joint enterprise, relate to all the charges in the indictment, including in particular those dealing with the treatment in the prison? If you -- you don't have to answer it now. You can let us know tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. We will be prepared to provide an answer by tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness B, you are reminded not to discuss your evidence with anybody, including members of the Prosecution team. We will adjourn until 9.30 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
